findings.title: updatecmd prints a warning on every successful Windows update, for the backup lock the library documents as expected
findings.description: After `Apply`, the `update` command calls `installed.Discard()` and turns any error into `inv.Warning("the previous binary is left at %s: %v", ...)`. On Windows the backup `<target>.old` is the file of the process running the update, so `Discard` returns `*BackupLockedError` on every update. The `Discard` doc comment and ADR-0031 both call that the normal outcome which "the caller may ignore", and the `UpdateCheckHooks` pre-run hook removes the file on the next command. The command does not separate that case from a real removal failure, so every successful self-update on Windows ends with a warning line on stderr.
findings.evidence:
updatecmd.go:256-259:
```go
backup := installed.Backup()
if err := installed.Discard(); err != nil {
    inv.Warning("the previous binary is left at %s: %v", backup, err)
}
```
install.go:209-211 returns `&BackupLockedError{Path: i.backup, Err: err}` when the resolved GOOS is windows and the remove fails with access denied or a sharing violation. ADR-0031, Consequences: "A Windows update leaves `<exe>.old` until the next run. `Discard` returns a `*BackupLockedError`, which the caller may ignore". source/update/example_unix_test.go:129 says the same: "A locked backup (*update.BackupLockedError) is not a failed update and may be ignored." The only test of this branch (`TestABackupThatCannotBeRemovedIsAWarning`) uses a directory at the backup path, not the locked case. Not run on Windows here; this follows from reading the code path.
findings.suggestion: Match `*update.BackupLockedError` with `errors.As` and stay silent (or print an info line saying the old binary is removed on the next run). Keep the warning for other `Discard` failures.

findings.title: `update --to` always fails for a custom Source that is not an AssetLocator, and only after the confirmation
findings.description: On the pinned path the command builds `update.Release{Tag: to}` itself, with nil `Assets`, and hands it to `Select`. `Select` treats nil `Assets` as "not listed" and requires the resolved Source to implement `AssetLocator`; otherwise it returns an error wrapping `ErrAssetsNotListed`. The `Source` interface has only `Latest(ctx, ch)`, so a custom Source that lists assets has no way to serve a named tag. For such a tool `--to` can never work, while the latest path does. The failure also comes after the downgrade guard and the `Update X from A to B?` prompt, so the user confirms an update that cannot start. The package doc and the command help describe `--to` without this limit.
findings.suggestion: Either document in updatecmd that `--to` needs a Source implementing `AssetLocator`, or run `Select` before the confirmation so the refusal comes first. An optional by-tag lookup interface for sources would close the gap fully.

findings.title: releasetest.Verify never extracts an archive, though its package doc says it checks the files a Config extracts
findings.description: The package doc says Verify "checks that the files in GoReleaser's dist directory are the ones a tool's update.Config downloads, verifies and extracts". Verify checks the tag, runs `Select` per built platform, verifies the minisign signature, and compares every listed SHA-256 digest. It never opens an archive. A dist whose archives carry the wrong binary name (for example a hand-edited `builds.binary`, or a missing `.exe` on windows), or use a format different from the extension in the name, passes Verify and the release-tool self-test. `Config.Extract` on the published release would then fail with `*BinaryNotFoundError`.
findings.evidence: verify.go:100-108 only records `sel.Archive.Name` under `sel.Checksums.Name`. `verifyChecksums` (202-238) reads the checksums file and signature, calls `minisign.Verify`, `checkDigest` for each listed file, and checks each archive name is listed. No code path calls `update.Config.Extract` or reads archive entries. The bullet list in doc.go (lines 6-16) also lists no extraction step, so the summary sentence at lines 1-4 overstates what is checked.
findings.suggestion: After the digest check, open each selected archive and assert it holds exactly one regular file named BinaryName (plus `.exe` for windows) in the format the Config derives. Otherwise drop "and extracts" from the package doc.

findings.title: The sh installer cannot find the latest release with BusyBox wget when curl is absent
findings.description: The script advertises "curl, else wget". The wget branch of `latest_location` passes `--max-redirect=0`, a GNU wget option that BusyBox wget (the wget of Alpine and most minimal images, which often have no curl) does not accept. BusyBox prints its usage text and exits non-zero, `|| :` hides the failure, no `  HTTP/` line reaches `wget.log`, and the script stops with "answered HTTP nothing, not a redirect to the latest release". With `<PREFIX>_VERSION` set the script works, because `fetch` uses only `-S -O`, which BusyBox supports. I could not run this: no BusyBox is installed in this environment, so it rests on BusyBox's option table, which has no `max-redirect` entry.
findings.evidence:
install.sh.in:92-93:
```sh
wget --max-redirect=0 -S -O /dev/null "$1" 2>"$tmp/wget.log" || :
_status=$(awk '/^  HTTP\// { s = $2 } END { print s }' "$tmp/wget.log")
```
then 100-103:
```sh
case $_status in
30[12378]) ;;
*) fail "$1 answered HTTP ${_status:-nothing}, not a redirect to the latest release" ;;
```
The downloader is chosen at 53-59 by `command -v wget` alone, with no check of which wget it is. Neither installscript/doc.go nor ADR-0023 lists GNU wget as a requirement.
findings.suggestion: For the wget fallback, either document that it needs GNU wget, or detect the missing option and fail with a message telling the user to set `<PREFIX>_VERSION` or install curl.
